title: Systematic investigation reveals extensive Epstein-Barr virus transcriptional regulation of the human genome.
journal: Cell Genomics, 2026 (PMC13477052). Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 200 (323,438 bytes). Article licence CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, read from the <permissions> block of the JATS XML. Dexheimer, Hass, Edsall, ... Kottyan, Weirauch (Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center). Preprint: bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.07.18.665561.
data_url: https://vtr.cchmc.org/ebv-vtr/data/ (open Apache directory index, no login). Raw data: GEO GSE303478 (public, 217 samples, released 2026-06-08). UCSC session: https://genome.ucsc.edu/s/Ledsall/vtr-ebv. Code: github.com/WeirauchLab plus Zenodo DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.20652060 (MARIO), 10.5281/zenodo.4266977 (RELI), 10.5281/zenodo.20671745 (nf-encode-atac), 10.5281/zenodo.20671763 (nf-encode-chip).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed, all HTTP 200: 14 manifest TSVs (4-52 KB), SHA1SUMS (188 B), ChIP-seq.hg38.tar.gz (3,425,064 B -> 13 narrowPeak files + README), ATAC-seq.hg38.tar.gz (19,192,821 B -> 10 narrowPeak + 36 BED + README), and all 9 per-vTR RNA differential-analysis tarballs (~11.5 MB each). ChIP narrowPeak files are uniformly 10 columns, 0 duplicate coordinates, 23 chromosomes: BMRF1 12,157 / RTA 8,164 / EBNA1 15,391 / EBNA2 10,079 / EBNA3A 3,108 / EBNA3B 8,460 / EBNA3C 1,579 / EBNALP 5,657 / ZTA 44,563 = 109,158 peaks; GFP-only control 319; RBPJ ChIP 3,744 (control) / 22,978 (+EBNA2) / 32,130 (+RTA). I merged the 9 vTR peak sets myself: 64,290 distinct regions, 62,340,273 bp (2.0% of the genome). ATAC IDR peaks 45,312-87,957 per vTR (GFP control 83,203). Differential ATAC BEDs are bare 3-column coordinates with NO effect size and NO FDR column (checked every file). My merges: all opening+closing = 243,046 events -> 109,533 distinct regions covering 97,127,999 bp; direct opening 26,852 -> 23,913 regions; direct closing 13,932 -> 9,493 regions. Each of the 9 DESeq2 result CSVs has exactly 61,544 rows and 9 columns (gene_id, gene_name, baseMean, log2FoldChange, lfcSE, pvalue, padj, classification, index), gene_id unique 61,544/61,544, gene_name only 60,308 unique. Significant gene counts: EBNALP 2,069, EBNA2 2,288, EBNA3C 2,451, EBNA3B 3,087, EBNA3A 3,811, RTA 5,160, ZTA 5,220, EBNA1 5,937, BMRF1 7,234; union 15,039 (24.44%); up/down split 45-55% each. Missingness measured in the BMRF1 table: pvalue NA 15,547/61,544, padj NA 32,192/61,544, classification = insignificant 22,118 / significant 7,234 / low_count 16,645 / zero_count 15,541 / outlier 6. Pairwise correlation of log2FoldChange across vTRs on the 15,039 union genes: min -0.131 (EBNA3B vs EBNALP), median 0.361, max 0.836 (EBNA3A vs EBNA3B). I built the candidate label table: of 109,158 vTR ChIP peaks, 37.8% overlap a 'direct' differential ATAC region, per-vTR 8.6% (RTA, EBNA1) to 60.1% (EBNA3A); that intersect ran in 0.4 s on this laptop. TPM file checked (RNA_cGFP_tagged_BMRF1_stable_transfection_all_reps.hg38.gene_tpm.tsv): 61,544 rows, 5 columns, 3 replicate columns, 0 NA. HTTP HEADs for files I did not download: RNA-seq.hg38.tar.gz 150,503,409 B, Supplemental_data_current.zip 228,286,240 B. Reference files named in Methods are live: GRCh38 primary assembly FASTA gz 844,691,642 B and gencode.v40.annotation.gtf.gz 48,043,727 B, both HTTP 200. GEO GSE303478 confirmed public via NCBI esummary (217 samples, Homo sapiens).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: From the paper, not confirmed in files: the 16 vTRs initially screened and why only 9 were taken forward; FRiP and TSS-enrichment quality numbers; the 90% EBNA3A/EBNA3B peak overlap and the 39% median pairwise overlap; the motif-enrichment results (AP-1 for ZTA and most others, CTCF for EBNA1/BMRF1/EBNALP, RBPJ for EBNA2/RTA); the ChromHMM chromatin-state distributions; the 5-fold enrichment of peaks near differentially expressed genes; the RTA-RBPJ interaction; the WNT3 CRISPR deletion; and the rheumatoid-arthritis GWAS/eQTL findings. Pipeline details (nf-core/rnaseq 3.11.1, STAR, Salmon 1.10.1, DESeq2 1.34.0, GENCODE 40, ENCODE ChIP/ATAC pipelines, IDR conservative peaks, DiffBind 3.12.0 at FDR 0.05, bedtools intersect for direct/indirect) are from the Methods text. NOT OPENED: RNA-seq.hg38.tar.gz (150 MB, over the 50 MB cap); Supplemental_data_current.zip (228 MB, over the cap); all BAM and bigWig files (raw/large); the HOMER knownResults HTML files (0.5-11 MB each, not needed yet); the deseq_vst-matrix.csv files (37.9 MB each, downloaded inside the tarballs but not parsed). The Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint returned HTTP 200 but the transfer stalled three times (26.5 MB, 40.8 MB, 80.7 MB of an unknown total), so Data S1-S9 were never opened. The GEO page at ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi returned a reCAPTCHA interstitial, so per-sample GEO metadata was taken from esummary only. One unresolved count gap: GEO reports 217 samples while the website manifests list 38 ChIP + 30 ATAC + 33 stable RNA + 106 transient RNA = 207, matching the paper's '139 RNA-seq, 30 ATAC-seq, 38 ChIP-seq'. Backbone licences (DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA, Nucleotide Transformer) were not re-verified in this session. The B-cell validation datasets (ZTA in Akata, EBNA2 in Ramos) are described in the paper; I did not retrieve their accessions.

a1_downloadable.note: Pass (checked in files). https://vtr.cchmc.org/ebv-vtr/data/ is an open Apache directory listing; ~25 GETs all returned HTTP 200 with no login, no registration and no access application. SHA1SUMS published. GEO GSE303478 is public. No controlled-access component. The only gap is that the website states no explicit data licence; the article is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Pass (checked in files), with one honest caveat. For the expression arm, log2FoldChange, lfcSE, padj and a 5-level classification column sit in each of the 9 DESeq2 CSVs (61,544 rows each, verified). For the chromatin arm the positive label sets are pre-computed files on the site (vTR_direct_opening.bed, vTR_direct_closing.bed), so the label is membership in a provided file; assigning the 'no change' class to the remaining ChIP peaks is a single interval intersect that I ran in 0.4 seconds. Nothing has to be inferred across independent sources.

a3_inputs_present.note: Pass with a note (checked). The DNA sequence is NOT in the files: peaks are hg38 coordinates only. Building inputs needs two bulk downloads that the Methods name with exact URLs and that I confirmed live: GRCh38 primary assembly FASTA (844,691,642 B) and gencode.v40.annotation.gtf.gz (48,043,727 B). That is two files, not thousands of lookups. narrowPeak column 10 (summit offset) is present in every row, so sequence windows can be centred properly.

a4_units_stated.note: Pass with a real caveat (checked). DESeq2 columns are self-describing and consistent: log2 fold change versus the GFP-only control cell line, baseMean as normalized counts, padj as Benjamini-Hochberg. TPM files are transcripts per million. But the peak files are headerless, so narrowPeak units (column 7 fold-enrichment, 8/9 -log10 p and q) are implied by format convention and the Methods, not written in the file. The differential ATAC BEDs carry no quantitative value at all: 3 columns, measured on all 36 files.

a5_enough_rows.note: Pass (counted in files). Primary task: 109,158 vTR ChIP peaks, of which 41,275 (37.8%) carry a chromatin-change label, split 8.6%-60.1% per viral protein. Expression arm: 553,896 gene-by-vTR rows (61,544 genes x 9 vTRs), 15,039 genes significant in at least one. Both are far above the 1,500-row bar.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: Measured: peaks and differential BEDs 22.6 MB compressed / ~118 MB extracted; nine DESeq2 result CSVs ~62 MB; TPM tables ~2.8 MB each. Add the hg38 reference: 806 MB gzipped, ~3.1 GB uncompressed. Total working set ~4 GB. Files deliberately skipped: RNA-seq.hg38.tar.gz 150 MB, Supplemental_data_current.zip 228 MB, all BAM/bigWig.
a6_fits_laptop.note: Pass (checked). Well under the ~5 GB bar, and the genome can be random-accessed with a FASTA index rather than loaded. No GPU needed: the baseline is cached frozen embeddings plus a linear or gradient-boosted head. This is a genomics paper whose usable working set is genuinely small because the authors published peak and differential tables, not just signal tracks.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Pass, and unusually strong (all recomputed from the files). Exact matches to the paper: 64,290 distinct vTR-occupied regions; 109,533 collectively opened or closed regions covering 97,127,999 bp; 23,913 direct opening and 9,493 direct closing regions; 15,039 differentially expressed genes (24%); the per-vTR range 2,069 (EBNALP) to 7,234 (BMRF1); ZTA 16,661 direct opening and 5,038 direct closing; BMRF1 5,787 direct closing; EBNA3C 24,723 indirect closing. Two small bookkeeping flaws found: GEO lists 217 samples against 207 in the website manifests and the paper; and vTR_EBV_RBPJ_ChIP.tsv / vTR_EBV_RBPJ_ChIP_vTR.tsv are byte-identical duplicates of the RNA-transient manifests, i.e. mislabelled index files.

a8_label_provenance.note: Pass, with three leakage traps I would write down before starting. Labels are physical measurements, not another model's output: expression labels are DESeq2 Wald tests on Salmon-quantified RNA-seq counts against a GFP-only control line; chromatin labels are DiffBind (FDR 0.05) on ENCODE-pipeline ATAC-seq peaks. Traps: (1) 'direct' is DEFINED as a differential ATAC peak intersecting that vTR's ChIP peak, so never use the vTR cell line's own ATAC signal as a feature - only the control line's accessibility; (2) baseMean is computed across both conditions and therefore partly contains the label, so use control-cell TPM instead; (3) the classification column encodes statistical power (low_count 16,645, zero_count 15,541 rows measured), so it must be a filter, never a feature.

B1.why: 81 files but keys are clean: hg38 coordinates and versioned Ensembl IDs; my interval join ran in 0.4 s.

B2.why: Every file parsed first try; narrowPeak uniformly 10 columns, BEDs 3, CSVs 9, no malformed rows.

B3.why: All nine use the same DESeq2 and DiffBind pipelines, but EBNALP's control is a different cell line (file name plus Methods).

B4.why: Measured 32,192 NA padj of 61,544, but the provided classification column makes the filter one line.

B5.why: Measured zero duplicate coordinates in all 61 peak/BED files; gene_id unique 61,544/61,544 in all nine CSVs.

B6.why: README is provenance plus checksums only; column meanings come from format convention and the paper, not a data dictionary.

C1.why: Informative either way: whether sequence predicts a binding site's chromatin consequence is a result in both directions.

C2.why: No model exists for EBV viral-regulator binding, but open human-TF models (maxATAC, scFAN, DNABERT-2 heads) serve the method.

C3.why: Clear novel plus unique-application angle: a week-old resource nobody has modelled, used for a transfer question across viral proteins.

C4.why: Each vTR needed an isogenic stable line plus ChIP, ATAC and triplicate RNA-seq; 207 libraries for nine proteins.

C5.why: Obvious dummies exist (majority class 62.2% unchanged, measured) plus the paper's own motif and enrichment numbers.

D1.why: DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA and Nucleotide Transformer are open-weight DNA models; data type is human genomic sequence, an exact match.

D2.why: Embed ~109k one-kilobase windows once on CPU, cache, fit a linear or boosted head; no fine-tuning needed.

D3.why: DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA repositories state permissive licences (not re-verified here); the article is CC BY-NC-ND; data licence unstated.

G1.why: hg38 coordinates in every peak file plus versioned Ensembl gene IDs and symbols in every expression table (checked).

G2.why: GWAS Catalog and eQTL Catalogue release 7 join on hg38 coordinates; the authors themselves did this for BMRF1.

G3.why: Interval overlap is inherently one-to-many (one peak hits several variants or elements); needs a stated collapse rule.

G4.why: Combination asks whether virus-hijacked elements are the same elements human variation disrupts; neither dataset answers that alone.

H1.why: GFP-only control line in every assay; closing as well as opening; 62.2% of binding sites measured as unchanged.

H2.why: One HEK293-derived Flp-In line, one lab, one viral protein over-expressed at a time; no B cells, no real infection.

H3.why: Claim is writable in one precise sentence because the cell line, assay, test and FDR threshold are all pinned down.

H4.why: The paper states the limitations outright: 'does not fully model physiologic vTR abundance' and 'candidate regulatory interactions'.

I1.why: Weirauch and Kottyan labs at Cincinnati Children's built the resource; Gewurz and Zhao at Harvard are co-authors.

I2.why: Ranking which of 109,158 binding sites are functional directly chooses which to test in infected B cells.

I3.why: The decision is a shortlist, so precision at top-k on a three-class call is the decision itself.

I4.why: A motif-plus-peak-strength rule may do most of the work; the paper already reports AP-1 opens and CTCF closes.

J1.why: Frozen DNA language model embeddings, grouped splits by chromosome and by viral protein, ablations, attribution.

J2.why: Known motif biology (AP-1, CTCF, RBPJ) and the 90% EBNA3A/EBNA3B peak overlap give built-in sanity checks.

J3.why: The joined site-by-label table is already useful on its own; I built it in 0.4 s and the counts match the paper.

J4.why: Four weeks is a sensible budget for this scope but it is not yet written down anywhere.

J5.why: No kill date or condition recorded in NOTES.md yet; must be added on day one.

E1.why: Hold out whole chromosomes (23 present, measured) and, separately, whole viral proteins; both prevent locus and protein leakage.

E2.why: 23 chromosomes and 9 viral proteins, smallest protein group 1,579 peaks; comfortably above five groups.

E3.why: Majority class is 62.2% unchanged (measured); per-vTR base rates 8.6%-60.1% give a strong per-group dummy.

E4.why: Three biological replicates per line with per-replicate TPM files (checked) and a per-gene lfcSE column (median 0.895).

E5.why: Model must recover AP-1 at opening and CTCF at closing sites, and must barely separate EBNA3A from EBNA3B.

E6.why: Label shuffling, dinucleotide-shuffled sequences, random embeddings of the same shape, and feature-block ablation all runnable.

E7.why: Published B-cell ChIP (ZTA in Akata, EBNA2 in Ramos) plus the resource's own 106-sample transient-transfection arm (file opened).

E8.why: No published machine-learning number for this task; I did reproduce all the paper's descriptive counts exactly.

existing_models.name: DeepEBV (Liang et al. 2021, Bioinformatics, doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab388) - an attention-based convolutional network that predicts where the Epstein-Barr virus genome physically inserts itself into human DNA.
existing_models.score_and_split: Abstract retrieved from Europe PMC only: trained and tested on the dsVIS integration-site database with repeat annotations and two-fold data augmentation, then validated on an independent dataset. No AUC figure was in the abstract and I did not open the full text; code availability not checked.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Abstract notes that integration preference depends strongly on the local genomic environment and that DNA-binding-protein motifs influence the signal; it does not address viral transcription-factor binding at all.

existing_models.name: DeepHTLV (Zeng et al. 2023, Patterns, PMC9982299) - a deep learning framework predicting human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 integration sites from genome sequence alone.
existing_models.score_and_split: Abstract only: reports 'high accuracy' with no number, eight motif clusters recovered. Split not described in the abstract; I did not open the full text.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Frames cis-regulatory control of integration-site choice as the open question. Again integration, not viral transcription-factor binding.

existing_models.name: maxATAC (Cazares et al. 2023, PLoS Comput Biol, doi 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010863) - deep neural networks predicting human transcription-factor binding from ATAC-seq accessibility.
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrieved as a search result with its abstract summary; I did not open the paper, so I have no AUPRC figure or split description. It is open-source and covers 127 human transcription factors - none of them viral.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Stated motivation is that suboptimal motif scanning remains the most common method for binding-site prediction from ATAC-seq. Generalisation to factors with no training data is the gap this project sits in.

existing_models.name: scFAN (Fu et al. 2020, Science Advances, doi 10.1126/sciadv.aba9031) and TAMC (Yuan et al. 2022, PLoS Comput Biol, doi 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009921) and Virtual ChIP-seq (Karimzadeh and Hoffman) - three open models predicting transcription-factor binding from accessibility, sequence and expression.
existing_models.score_and_split: Known from search-result abstracts only; no numbers or splits retrieved. All are trained on human factors with large ENCODE-scale ChIP-seq training sets; none has ever seen a viral transcription factor.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The common theme in their framing is cell-type transfer for factors with existing ChIP data; predicting the functional consequence of a binding event (does it change accessibility?) is not what they do.

existing_models.name: GLNet-TFBS (2026, doi 10.1007/s12539-025-00807-2) and DNABERT-Enhancer (2026, PMC13579158) - representative recent DNABERT-2-based heads for binding-site and enhancer classification.
existing_models.score_and_split: Abstracts retrieved via Europe PMC. DNABERT-Enhancer reports 88.05% accuracy and Matthews correlation 0.76 on an independent set of 21,926 / 46,159 ENCODE enhancers. GLNet-TFBS gives no number in the abstract. Both are human-only, both are classification against background rather than functional consequence.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: DNABERT-Enhancer's stated gap is the absence of consistent signatures distinguishing regulatory regions from other genomic regions - exactly the ambiguity this dataset resolves experimentally.

existing_models.name: No model found for the actual task.
existing_models.score_and_split: Searches run: Europe PMC keyword and preprint-restricted queries for Epstein-Barr virus combined with deep learning / language model / machine learning and transcription factor or chromatin (28 preprint hits, none relevant); two web searches on viral transcription-factor binding prediction and on predicting which binding events are functional. Nothing predicts EBV viral-regulator occupancy or its chromatin consequence in the human genome. Likely novel, not proven novel.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: This paper's own Discussion names the open problems: effects are measured one viral protein at a time, in a 293-derived over-expression system, and the binding events 'should be interpreted as candidate regulatory interactions that require confirmation in infection models'.

backbone.name: DNABERT-2 (a 117-million-parameter transformer pretrained on multi-species genomes, open weights on Hugging Face) as the primary backbone, embedding the one-kilobase window centred on each peak summit. HyenaDNA-tiny-1k and Nucleotide Transformer v2-50M are the fallbacks; a dinucleotide-shuffled-sequence embedding and a random-vector embedding of the same shape are mandatory controls. Not proposed: AlphaFold (a structure predictor) or any diffusion generator.
backbone.hardware: 16 GB laptop CPU. Embed roughly 109,000 one-kilobase windows once (about 6 CPU-hours estimated at ~5 windows per second), cache to disk as float32 (109,158 x 768 is about 335 MB), then fit logistic regression or gradient boosting in minutes. No GPU at any stage.
backbone.licence: Article CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (verified in the JATS permissions block). The data website states no explicit licence - resolve this with the lead contact before redistributing derived tables. DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA are stated as permissively licensed on their repositories but I did not re-verify in this session; Nucleotide Transformer v2 is non-commercial.

integration.partner_dataset: GWAS Catalog (the authors used the 2026-02-18 release) plus eQTL Catalogue release 7 - the paper already ran exactly this join for BMRF1 peaks with its RELI tool and found enrichment at rheumatoid-arthritis risk variants, so the join is pre-validated. Secondary partners on the same key: ENCODE candidate cis-regulatory elements and the HEK293 ChromHMM state map the paper used.
integration.join_key: hg38 genomic coordinates (present in every peak and BED file, genome build confirmed in the Methods as GRCh38/hg38) for the variant and element partners; versioned Ensembl gene IDs (61,544 unique per table, checked) for GTEx, Open Targets and the eQTL target side. No new identifier mapping needs to be built.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Are the human regulatory elements that Epstein-Barr virus proteins land on and switch on or off the same elements where common human genetic variation changes gene expression and raises autoimmune-disease risk?

controls.positive_control: (1) Motif recovery: a working model must attribute chromatin opening to AP-1-like sequences and closing to CTCF sequences, and must find RBPJ sequences under EBNA2 and RTA peaks - the paper states all three in advance, and the per-vTR HOMER result files are downloadable. (2) EBNA3A and EBNA3B share about 90% of their peaks (paper) and their expression effects correlate at r = 0.836 (I measured this), so the model should be nearly unable to tell them apart while separating ZTA from EBNA1 easily. (3) Trivially learnable target: predict GC content or peak width from the same sequence window - this must come out near-perfect or the plumbing is wrong.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the open/close/unchanged labels globally and then within chromosome, and confirm collapse to the 62.2% majority-class dummy. Replace sequences with dinucleotide-preserving shuffles. Replace embeddings with random vectors of identical shape. Ablate feature blocks one at a time: sequence only, peak strength only, control-cell accessibility only - if peak strength alone does the work, that is the finding. Also score the 319 GFP-only control ChIP peaks, which should look non-functional.
controls.external_validation: Within the resource: the 106-sample transient-transfection arm is an independent experimental system from the stable lines (I opened EBNA3C_transient_test and confirmed three separate DESeq2 comparisons), and EBNALP's different control line is a built-in batch probe. Outside: the published ZTA ChIP-seq in EBV-negative Akata B cells and EBNA2 ChIP-seq in EBV-infected Ramos B cells that the paper compares against (accessions not retrieved by me) give a true cell-type transfer test. Cross-virus: Kaposi's sarcoma herpesvirus RTA, which shares only 25% amino-acid identity with EBV RTA. No publication-year column exists, so no temporal split.

honest_claim_h3: Among the 109,158 sites where one of nine individually over-expressed Epstein-Barr virus proteins binds the genome of a single HEK293-derived Flp-In cell line in one laboratory, the model predicts which sites show a DiffBind-significant (FDR 0.05) change in chromatin accessibility; it says nothing about EBV-infected B cells, about combinations of viral proteins acting together, about physiological viral protein levels, or about sites where the assay had too little power to call a change.

pitch.headline: 109,158 viral-protein binding sites in human DNA, 37.8% with a measured chromatin-opening or closing label, every headline count reproduced from the files
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Nine Epstein-Barr virus regulators were each profiled separately and paired with accessibility changes, and the authors published peak and differential tables rather than only signal tracks, so the usable working set is about 4 GB instead of terabytes. Twelve of the paper's headline numbers — 64,290 distinct binding regions, 109,533 opened-or-closed regions over 97,127,999 bp, 23,913 direct opening, 9,493 direct closing, 15,039 differentially expressed genes — recomputed to the exact digit from the downloaded files.
pitch.the_win: A frozen DNABERT-2 head that beats the motif-plus-peak-strength baseline by more than 0.02 macro-F1 on chromosome-held-out splits, and transfers under leave-one-viral-protein-out — a number for a task no existing model addresses, since searches found nothing predicting EBV viral-regulator occupancy or its chromatin consequence.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: Something is learned either way: if peak strength and motifs alone match the sequence model, that is the finding — a viral protein's effect on DNA packaging is not written in the sequence it sits on but decided by the cell's pre-existing state. That check is also the cheapest experiment, runnable on a label table that already builds in 0.4 seconds before the genome is downloaded.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Weirauch and Kottyan groups at Cincinnati Children's, who built the resource and state in their own Discussion that these binding events are candidate interactions requiring confirmation in infection models — a ranked shortlist decides which of the 109,158 sites are worth testing in genuinely infected B cells. The autoimmune-genetics community has a second stake, since the paper already joined BMRF1 peaks to rheumatoid-arthritis risk variants (that join reported in the paper's text, not re-run by me).

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the human DNA sequence under a site where an Epstein-Barr virus protein lands to predict whether chromatin there opens or closes.
plain_idea.train_on: One example per binding site: 109,158 sites in total, from nine viral proteins (1,579 to 44,563 sites each), a count I measured in the downloaded files. Each example is about 1,000 DNA letters centred on the site, plus how strong the binding signal was and how loosely packed that stretch of DNA already was in control cells that carried no viral protein.
plain_idea.predict: One of three outcomes: the DNA there becomes more loosely packed, more tightly packed, or does not measurably change. The truth comes from ATAC-seq, a laboratory assay that cuts DNA wherever it is loose enough to reach, compared between cells making the viral protein and control cells and tested with a standard statistical tool at a 5% false-discovery rate. I counted the answers myself: 37.8% of sites are labelled as changed, ranging from 8.6% to 60.1% depending on which viral protein.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Epstein-Barr virus infects more than nine in ten adults and is tied to multiple sclerosis, lupus and several cancers; the laboratory that built this resource needs to know which of its hundred thousand binding sites are worth the expense of testing in genuinely infected B cells, and a ranked shortlist is directly usable. If the model fails, that is also worth knowing: it would say a viral protein's effect on DNA packaging is not written in the sequence it sits on but is decided by the cell's pre-existing state.

ml_idea: A 109,158-row three-class problem built entirely from files I already downloaded. Features: frozen DNABERT-2 embeddings of the one-kilobase window centred on each peak summit (narrowPeak column 10, present in every row), plus peak fold-enrichment and width, distance to the nearest GENCODE v40 transcription start site, and the control cell line's accessibility and ChromHMM state. Label: opening / closing / unchanged, from the supplied direct_opening and direct_closing BED files against the full ChIP peak set. Two splits that matter: grouped cross-validation holding out whole chromosomes, and leave-one-viral-protein-out to ask whether what is learned from eight transfers to the ninth. Benchmark against a motif-plus-peak-strength logistic regression, because the paper already reports that AP-1 marks opening and CTCF marks closing. Extension, not the core: join peak-to-gene by transcription start site and predict the direction of the log2 fold change from the 553,896-row expression matrix.

effort.compute_note: Download sizes are HTTP Content-Length values I read directly. The interval intersect over 109,158 peaks against the differential BEDs was timed on this laptop at 0.4 s, and parsing all nine 61,544-row DESeq2 tables took a few seconds. The 6 CPU-hours for DNABERT-2 over ~109k one-kilobase windows is an estimate at roughly 5 windows per second and was NOT timed; likewise the 20-minute cross-validation figure and the 6 GB peak RAM, which assumes the genome is read through a FASTA index rather than loaded.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Fit logistic regression on four cheap features - peak fold-enrichment, peak width, distance to the nearest GENCODE v40 transcription start site, and AP-1 plus CTCF motif scores - on the 109,158-row three-class table that already exists (I built it in 0.4 s). If that lands within about 0.02 macro-F1 of a frozen DNA-language-model head, the sequence model adds nothing and the project is a one-page note rather than a project. Do this before downloading the genome.

verdict_reason: Every Part A killer was checked in the files, not read in the paper, and the resource is the most faithfully reproducible one I have audited: 64,290 distinct binding regions, 109,533 opened-or-closed regions over 97,127,999 bp, 23,913 direct opening and 9,493 direct closing events, and 15,039 differentially expressed genes all recomputed to the exact digit the paper reports. Despite being a virology-genomics paper, the usable working set is about 4 GB (mostly the hg38 reference), because the authors published peak and differential tables rather than only signal tracks; the label table exists in 0.4 seconds of compute and the class balance is a healthy 37.8% positive. Three things drive the verdict: no model exists for EBV viral-regulator binding while open human-transcription-factor models supply ready baselines; a specific open DNA backbone fits with cached CPU embeddings; and the single genuine risk - that a motif-plus-peak-strength rule already solves it (I4 = 1) - is itself the first and cheapest experiment. Watch the two real weaknesses: one HEK293 cell line and one lab (H2 = 0, so the honest claim is narrow), and the A8 trap that 'direct' is defined as the ChIP-ATAC intersection, so the vTR line's own accessibility signal must never be a feature.
